newsitem.title: USA: Wary reaction to tobacco deal - "devil in details".
newsitem.headline: Wary reaction to tobacco deal - "devil in details".

text.p: From senators and doctors to lobbyists and race car drivers, Friday's historic tobacco deal sparked wary calls for prudence and sober reminders that the devil is in the details.

Broadly, the tentative agreement between the tobacco industry and state negotiators requires tobacco firms to pay $368.5 billion, admit that tobacco is addictive and submit to extensive new government regulation.

In return, the state attorneys general who forged the settlement during months of tortuous negotiations with company executives, promised them immunity from any further punitive liability for past deception, fraud or conspiracy.
Among members of Congress, who must approve the agreement, satisfaction was muted by a healthy dose of skepticism and assurances that it would be carefully picked apart.
"The devil is in the details," said Iowa Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin. "This deal now needs to emerge from the smoke-filled rooms into the sunshine of the public arena."

Sen. Edward Kennedy said the tobacco industry had gotten off too lightly and noted the "glaring omission" of a substantial payment to the federal government for costs incurred by federal health programs.

"Given the track record of deceit, manipulation and bad faith by the tobacco industry, there is every reason to be skeptical of any agreement which the tobacco industry is willing to support," the Massachusetts Democrat said.
Health groups agree on long-term goals for tobacco control but are not speaking with one voice on this settlement.
The American Cancer Society and the American Medical Association have been supportive of settlement efforts, but both reacted cautiously and mildly Friday.
The American Cancer Society expressed encouragement with the public health concepts of the settlement but refused to take a final position "until we complete an extensive review."
"We want a settlement to further our mission in bringing cancer under control as a major health problem," the society said.
The AMA called the deal "a significant first step," but warned of "the cruel betrayal" perpetrated by the tobacco industry in the past.

"We strongly urge the American people to take a close look at the range of concessions being made by the industry and ask themselves, 'Will this plan save lives, will it provide measurably better protections for our kids than could be realistically achieved otherwise?'" the AMA said.

Other prominent groups, among them the American Lung Association and smaller anti-smoking activist groups, were more skeptical, and feared that the industry would be able to reshape any settlement to its own advantage in Congress.

"The tobacco companies have been weakened over the past 10 to 20 years ... But if they are going to pay out some $300 billion or $400 billion, they aren't going to worry about a billion or a half-billion to do some lobbying," said John Banzhaf, executive director of Action of Smoking and Health.

Banzhaf critcized the deal for failing to provide "full and unfettered" power to the Food and Drug Admimnistration to regulate nicotine, particulary the 12-year lag before the FDA would be able to take steps to eliminate it entirely.

The National Association for Stock Car Auto Racing, whose sponsorship by tobacco companies would be ended under the settlement, noted that it had had "a mutually beneficial relationship" with the industry for more than 30 years.
"We have not had an opportunity to review the proposed agreement so it would be premature to speculate on what effect this will hove on motor sports," NASCAR said.
